L'Anse aux Meadows. A Norse settlement on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada, dating to around 1000 CE, representing the only confirmed pre-Columbian European presence in North America. Discovered archaeologically in 1960, the remains of Viking structures and Norse artifacts provided the first definitive proof that Vikings reached the Americas five centuries before Columbus, matching descriptions in Norse sagas of a legendary land called Vinland.

The settlement was located at the tip of the Great Northern Peninsula in Newfoundland, discovered by Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad and his wife, archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad, in 1960. The site contains the remains of eight Norse-built structures known as longhouses, constructed from sod laid over wooden frames—similar to Viking buildings found in Greenland and Iceland.

Radiocarbon dating places the occupation around 1000 CE, during the time of Leif Erikson, the Norse explorer traditionally credited in medieval sagas with discovering Vinland. Archaeological finds include distinctly Norse artifacts: iron nails, tools, a weaving loom, and notably, the only known Viking spindle whorl ever found outside Scandinavia—artifacts that confirmed the European origin of the settlement.

The site shows evidence of Norse iron-working, food storage, and habitation, but was apparently occupied for only a brief period, estimated at between ten and twenty years, before being mysteriously abandoned. The Icelandic sagas Grönlendinga saga and Eirík's saga contain narrative accounts of voyages to Vinland, providing historical context that matches the archaeological discovery. The settlement was likely a way-station or trading post between Greenland and indigenous North American peoples, though the reasons for its sudden abandonment remain unclear, a puzzle that continues to fascinate scholars today.
